concepts: Terms of a G.P. as sides of a triangle
questions.question: If three successive terms of a G.P. with common ratio $r\ (r>1)$ are the lengths of the sides of a triangle and $[r]$ denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to $r$, then $3[r]+[-r]$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: For $r>1$ the largest side is $ar$, so only the sum of the two smaller sides needs checking: it gives $r^2-r-1<0$.
solution: Let the three terms of the G.P. be $\frac{a}{r},\ a,\ ar$ with $r>1$ and $a>0$; the largest is $ar$.
For a triangle, the sum of the two smaller sides must exceed the third: $\frac{a}{r}+a>ar$.
Divide by $a>0$ and multiply by $r>0$: $1+r>r^2$, i.e. $r^2-r-1<0$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Avoid the surds: with sides $1,r,r^2$ the polynomial $f(r)=r^2-r-1$ changes sign between $1$ and $2$, which pins down both floors.
solution: Since $r>1$, the largest side is the third term; the condition is $f(r)=r^2-r-1<0$ (sides scaled to $1,\ r,\ r^2$).
$f(1)=-1<0$ and $f(2)=1>0$, and $f$ is increasing for $r>\frac12$, so the root lies in $(1,2)$.
Because $f(r)<0$ and $f$ is increasing on $r>1$, we get $1<r<\text{(root)}<2$; hence $[r]=1$.
For a non-integer $x$, $[-x]=-[x]-1$; $r$ is not an integer, so $[-r]=-1-1=-2$.

useful_results: Sides in G.P. $a,ar,ar^2$ with $r>1$ form a triangle iff $r^2<r+1$, i.e. $1<r<\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}$ (the golden ratio). For $r<1$ the condition is $r>\frac{\sqrt5-1}{2}$ (symmetric about $r\to1/r$).
For non-integer $x$: $[x]+[-x]=-1$; for integer $x$: $[x]+[-x]=0$. Use it to evaluate $[-x]$ at once.
To locate a root of a polynomial inequality for floor-type questions, a sign check at consecutive integers ($f(1)<0<f(2)$) is enough; no surds are needed.

concepts: Roots of a quadratic equation and power sums
questions.question: If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the roots of the equation $x^2-7x-1=0$, then the value of $\frac{\alpha^{21}+\beta^{21}+\alpha^{17}+\beta^{17}}{\alpha^{19}+\beta^{19}}$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: Each root satisfies $x^{n+2}=7x^{n+1}+x^n$, so the power sums $S_n=\alpha^n+\beta^n$ obey the same recurrence.
solution: Multiplying by $\alpha^{n}$, $\beta^n$ and adding (Newton's theorem), with $S_n=\alpha^n+\beta^n$: $S_{n+2}-7S_{n+1}-S_n=0$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use $\alpha\beta=-1$: then $\alpha^{-2}=\beta^2$, so the numerator factors as $\alpha^{19}(\alpha^2+\beta^2)+\beta^{19}(\beta^2+\alpha^2)$.
solution: So the numerator is $(\alpha^2+\beta^2)(\alpha^{19}+\beta^{19})$ and the ratio equals $\alpha^2+\beta^2$.

useful_results: Power sums of the roots of $x^2-px+q=0$ satisfy $S_{n+2}=pS_{n+1}-qS_n$ with $S_0=2,\ S_1=p$; here $p=7,\ q=-1$.

questions.question: Let $M$ denote the set of all real matrices of order $3\times3$ and let $S=\{-3,-2,-1,1,2\}$. Let $S_1=\{A=[a_{ij}]\in M: A=A^T \text{ and } a_{ij}\in S\ \forall\ i,j\}$, $S_2=\{A=[a_{ij}]\in M: A=-A^T \text{ and } a_{ij}\in S\ \forall\ i,j\}$, $S_3=\{A=[a_{ij}]\in M: a_{11}+a_{22}+a_{33}=0 \text{ and } a_{ij}\in S\ \forall\ i,j\}$. If $n(S_1\cup S_2\cup S_3)=125\alpha$, then $\alpha$ equals ______.
questions.key_idea: A skew-symmetric matrix has zero diagonal and $0\notin S$, so $S_2=\varnothing$; only $S_1\cup S_3$ is left, via inclusion–exclusion.
solution: Write $A=[a_{ij}]$ with nine entries, each chosen from $S$ ($n(S)=5$).
$S_3$: the diagonal $(a_{11},a_{22},a_{33})$ must sum to $0$. The only multisets from $S$ are $\{1,2,-3\}$, $\{1,1,-2\}$, $\{-1,-1,2\}$.
These give $3!=6$, $3$ and $3$ ordered triples, i.e. $12$ diagonals; the other six entries are free: $n(S_3)=12\times5^6$.
$S_1\cap S_3$: symmetric with trace $0$: $12$ diagonals and only 3 free off-diagonal entries, so $n(S_1\cap S_3)=12\times5^3$.
questions.correction_note: Gap, answer unchanged: the PDF does not say that n(S1 ∩ S2) = 0 (so S2 contributes nothing to the union) and does not justify the three diagonal multisets; both added, plus the explicit alpha = 13*125 - 12. The PDF also ends with a stray 'alpha/beta = 15' that belongs to another question (beta is not defined here); dropped. Brute force: 12 diagonals, union = 201625 = 125*1613.

alternate_solutions.idea: Split the union into two disjoint pieces: all of $S_3$, plus the symmetric matrices that are not in $S_3$ (trace $\neq0$), so no intersection is subtracted.
solution: Since $S_2=\varnothing$, the union is $S_1\cup S_3$, which is the disjoint union $S_3\ \cup\ (S_1\setminus S_3)$.
Diagonals: $5^3=125$ ordered triples in all, of which $12$ have sum $0$, so $113$ have non-zero trace.
$n(S_1\setminus S_3)$: symmetric matrices with trace $\neq0$: $113$ diagonals $\times$ $5^3$ off-diagonals $=14125$.

useful_results: A real skew-symmetric matrix has zero diagonal; if $0$ is not an allowed entry, the set of such matrices is empty. A symmetric $n\times n$ matrix has $\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$ free entries (6 for $n=3$), a skew-symmetric one $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ (3 for $n=3$).
Counting with a condition on a part of the entries (such as the trace): count the allowed diagonals separately and multiply by the number of free choices of the remaining entries.
Number of ordered triples from $\{-3,-2,-1,1,2\}$ summing to 0 is $12$; in general sort by multiset and count $3!$, $3$ or $1$ arrangements.
$n(A\cup B)=n(A)+n(B)-n(A\cap B)$ and its disjoint form $n(A\cup B)=n(B)+n(A\setminus B)$ are interchangeable; pick whichever needs fewer new counts.
